item.title: Broadcom CEO likens AI boom to a casino even as he targets $230 billion in chip sales
item.description:
Coming from one of the AI boom’s biggest beneficiaries, Tan’s remarks give weight to the bubble debate and may encourage investors to separate companies with proven AI returns from those relying on speculative demand. The warning that financing could become the binding constraint shifts the focus from chip supply to credit, putting AI-linked debt deals, lessor structures and the balance sheets of capital-hungry model developers under closer scrutiny. Broadcom’s own role in backing the $60 billion Anthropic-linked package adds counterparty risk to its story that the market may begin to price. For semiconductor stocks, the message is mixed: demand remains intact, but questions about customer profitability and funding introduce a longer-term risk to forecasts.

---

Earlier:

  • JPMorgan says Q3 earnings will support stocks as growth spreads beyond AI

---

The man selling the shovels says many of the prospectors have no idea what they are digging for, and he is now helping lend them the money to keep digging.

Summary:

  • Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said at an event in Singapore on Monday that many AI investors do not understand what they are investing in and likened their behaviour to casino gambling, Bloomberg reported
  • He compared companies experimenting with AI to children burning through arcade tokens without learning anything, and questioned OpenAI’s long-term profitability despite annualised revenue of around $50 billion
  • Broadcom’s AI semiconductor revenue more than tripled to around $17 billion in its fiscal third quarter, and it expects about $22 billion in the fourth quarter
  • Tan forecasts annual AI chip revenue rising roughly fourfold from about $58 billion this fiscal year to $230 billion in fiscal 2028, with OpenAI and Anthropic among key customers
  • He warned access to financing, rather than memory chip shortages, could become the industry’s biggest constraint
  • Banks last week began syndicating a $60 billion AI financing package tied to Anthropic’s lease of Google-designed chips, including $42 billion in loans backed by Broadcom’s credit rating, the Financial Times reported

Broadcom Chief Executive Hock Tan has warned that many investors piling into artificial intelligence do not understand what they are buying, comparing the boom to a casino even as his company forecasts AI chip revenue reaching $230 billion a year by fiscal 2028.

Speaking at an event in Singapore on Monday, Tan said a lot of investors have “no clue” what they are investing in, according to Bloomberg. He said investors had set very extreme expectations, only to find that investing in AI felt almost like gambling. Tan also questioned whether businesses are getting real value from the technology, likening companies experimenting with AI to children who spend their arcade tokens quickly without learning anything.

His scepticism extended to the developers selling AI services. Tan said OpenAI’s annualised revenue of around $50 billion in September showed strong demand, but argued that its enormous training costs give little sign of long-term profitability.

The comments stand out because few companies have gained more from the AI investment wave than Broadcom, which designs custom AI chips and data centre networking equipment for customers including OpenAI and Anthropic. Its AI semiconductor revenue more than tripled from a year earlier to around $17 billion in the fiscal third quarter, and the company expects about $22 billion in the fourth quarter. Tan forecasts annual AI chip revenue will rise roughly fourfold, from about $58 billion this fiscal year to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Part of that growth depends on OpenAI, the same company whose path to profit he has now called into question.

Tan said the industry’s biggest constraint may soon be access to capital rather than shortages of memory chips. Broadcom is itself becoming more involved in financing the build-out. Banks last week began syndicating a $60 billion AI financing package tied to Anthropic’s lease of Google-designed chips, including $42 billion of senior loans supported by Broadcom’s credit rating, the Financial Times reported. Such arrangements can help turn chip demand into sales, but they also expose Broadcom to added financial risk if customers struggle to meet their commitments.

The remarks sharpen a debate that has followed the AI trade for months. If demand for computing power is not in doubt, the question becomes whether the companies buying it can generate the returns, and the funding, needed to keep paying. Investors will look to Broadcom’s next results for any sign of how its financing exposure is evolving and whether customer commitments remain on track.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UK retail sales beat forecasts but fuel bill jump of 17% shows squeeze on shoppers
item.description:
The data offer little to change the picture for sterling or gilts on their own, but the mix carries a stagflationary edge: households are spending more on fuel while volumes in discretionary categories stay subdued. A near-17% jump in fuel spending shows how the oil and diesel shock is feeding into household budgets, which keeps upside risk on UK inflation even as underlying demand looks soft. For UK retailers, weak non-food sales and consumers trimming non-essential spending point to a cautious run into the key Christmas trading period. The 28 October budget is the next catalyst, with any tax rises likely to weigh further on discretionary spending.

---

British shoppers spent a little more in September, but much of it went into the fuel tank and the pub, not the high street.

Summary:

  • BRC like-for-like sales rose 1.0% year on year in September, above the 0.7% expected and up from 0.5% in August; total sales rose 1.3%, below the 12-month average of 1.5%
  • Food sales rose 2.5% while non-food edged up just 0.3%; health and beauty had its best month of the year, but warm weather hurt clothing and footwear
  • Barclays card spending growth slowed slightly to 2.0% from 2.1%, with essential spending up 2.5% on a near-17% jump in fuel spending as diesel prices hit record highs
  • Spending at bars, pubs and clubs rose nearly 4%, a fourth straight monthly gain, helped by summer weather that lasted through most of September
  • Barclays’ gauge of confidence in household finances hit a seven-month high of 67%, but 68% of consumers are concerned about the 28 October budget and 30% are cutting back on non-essentials

UK retail sales growth picked up more than expected in September, but the detail of two consumer surveys published on Tuesday suggests households are not so much spending more as paying more, with record diesel prices absorbing a growing share of budgets.

The British Retail Consortium said like-for-like sales, which strip out changes in store space, rose 1.0% from a year earlier, beating forecasts of 0.7% and doubling August’s 0.5% pace. Total sales rose 1.3%, up from 0.7% in August but still below the 12-month average of 1.5%. The BRC measures sales by value rather than volume, so the gains include the effect of higher prices.

The split between categories tells the story. Food sales rose 2.5%, while non-food sales barely moved, up 0.3%. Health and beauty had its strongest month of the year, and toys got a lift from products marking Pokemon’s 30th anniversary. Clothing and footwear had a weak month as unseasonably warm weather delayed the switch to autumn wardrobes. BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said households remained cautious ahead of expected increases in bills and taxes.

A separate survey from Barclays, based on card spending data, showed annual growth slowing slightly to 2.0% from 2.1%. Essential spending rose 2.5%, driven by a jump of around 17% in fuel spending after diesel prices hit record highs, a reminder of how the global energy shock is filtering through to household budgets. Non-essential spending rose 1.8%. The warm weather was good news for hospitality, with spending at bars, pubs and clubs up nearly 4% for a fourth consecutive monthly gain.

Consumer sentiment sends mixed signals. Barclays said confidence in household finances rose to a seven-month high of 67%. Yet 68% of consumers said they were worried about how finance minister John Healey’s budget on 28 October would affect them, and 30% said they were cutting back on non-essential spending.

The two surveys also cover different periods, which helps explain why they appear to move in opposite directions. The BRC data run from 30 August to 3 October, capturing the start of autumn, while the Barclays figures cover 22 August to 24 September.

With fuel costs eating into disposable income and the budget only weeks away, the next few months will test whether improving confidence translates into spending beyond essentials, particularly as retailers head into the crucial Christmas period.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs sees three ways to rein in French bond spread as oil and politics weigh
item.description:
Goldman’s framing makes the French spread partly an oil trade, so escalation in the Middle East, including the Saudi-Houthi confrontation and stalled US-Iran talks, now feeds directly into French borrowing costs through the energy and neutral-rate channel. That links European sovereign risk to crude in a way that could amplify any supply shock. The view that the ECB needs far more market disorder before acting suggests investors should not count on an official backstop, leaving the spread vulnerable to headline swings until the 2027 election cycle. A constructive stance on core European rates, combined with neutrality on France, points to relative value trades favouring Bunds and other core markets over French debt while uncertainty persists.

---

Goldman reckons France’s bond spread is now hostage to oil, the ECB and the 2027 ballot box, and none of those is likely to come to the rescue soon.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says an initial rise in rates driven by high energy prices has become more structural on strong data, lifting estimates of the neutral rate
  • Higher borrowing costs weigh hardest on heavily indebted France, whose debt-to-GDP ratio was 119% in the second quarter, according to the national statistics institute
  • The bank sees three possible brakes on spread widening: a sharp fall in oil prices, a dovish ECB shift such as slower quantitative tightening, or a credible fiscal plan after the May 2027 presidential election
  • Goldman cautions that oil depends on Middle East developments, that ECB action would likely need much more market disorder, and that the fiscal fix is still some way off
  • It is neutral on French rates, saying the widening offers some value but the outlook is uncertain, and constructive on European rates overall given its benign inflation view

France’s sharp bond market repricing reflects a rate shock that began with energy prices and has since become more entrenched, according to Goldman Sachs, which sees only a handful of ways to bring the French-German spread back under control.

In a note setting out three questions on the widening, the bank said the initial rise in rates driven by elevated energy prices has turned more structural as strong economic data push up estimates of the neutral interest rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. Goldman said higher borrowing costs can be particularly punishing for heavily indebted countries such as France, whose debt-to-GDP ratio reached 119% in the second quarter of 2026, according to the national statistics institute.

The bank said rising French yields point to growing market concern about the country’s fiscal path, particularly in a higher-for-longer rate environment and with political uncertainty building ahead of next year’s presidential election. The French premium over German debt reached its widest level since the 2011 eurozone debt crisis earlier this month, at close to 160 basis points, before easing back toward the 130s, according to market reports.

Goldman identified three developments that could rein in the widening. The first is a sharp fall in oil prices, which would naturally pull bond yields lower, though the bank cautioned this cannot be relied on given its dependence on events in the Middle East. The second is a dovish shift from the European Central Bank to ease financial conditions, which Goldman said could come without rate cuts, for example by slowing quantitative tightening. It added, however, that markets would likely need to become much more disorderly before such tools are used. ECB officials have so far signalled that intervention is not yet warranted. The third is an improving fiscal outlook, with a credible consolidation plan after the May 2027 presidential election and the parliamentary elections likely to follow. Goldman noted this remains relatively distant.

On positioning, Goldman said it is neutral on French rates. The spread widening has created some value, it said, but the situation remains uncertain. Across Europe more broadly, the bank holds a constructive view on rates, arguing that the degree of monetary tightening priced in is unwarranted given its benign inflation outlook.

With oil exposed to Middle East risk, the ECB reluctant to step in and the fiscal reset tied to an election more than six months away, the bank’s analysis suggests French spreads may stay sensitive to headlines well into next year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More on Standard Chartered adding RLUSD custody in Dubai, eyes LMAX collateral link for clients
item.description:
The announcement is more a signal about market structure than a price catalyst. Bank custody does not create direct demand for RLUSD or for XRP, and traders should not read it that way. The bigger question is competition. If regulated banks start offering off-exchange margin, smaller stablecoins with bank backing could win institutional business that has so far gone to the largest tokens. Venues may also come under pressure to offer similar setups once a mirrored model proves itself, which could change how collateral moves across crypto trading.

---

Earlier:

  • Standard Chartered custody for Ripple’s RLUSD: what custody and collateral mirroring mean for traders

---

Standard Chartered is offering to hold Ripple’s stablecoin and let clients trade against it without the tokens ever reaching an exchange, but the trading half of that promise still needs regulators to sign off.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered now offers institutional custody of RLUSD on the XRP Ledger through its DIFC branch, regulated by the DFSA.
  • A planned integration with LMAX Group would make RLUSD eligible collateral on agreed LMAX products through “collateral mirroring.”
  • Under mirroring, the tokens stay at the bank while LMAX credits their value toward client positions.
  • The LMAX leg is not live and still needs final documentation, testing and regulatory approval, with no launch date given.
  • RLUSD has a market value of about $2.45 billion, under 1% of a roughly $306 billion stablecoin market.
  • The bank has offered crypto custody in Dubai since 2024 and in July began letting institutions mint and redeem USDC directly.

Standard Chartered has begun offering institutional custody for Ripple’s dollar-backed stablecoin RLUSD through its branch in the Dubai International Financial Centre, and is preparing a link with LMAX Group that would let clients use the tokens as trading collateral without moving them off the bank’s books. The British lender said on Monday that eligible clients can now hold the XRP Ledger version of RLUSD on its digital asset custody infrastructure, with the service run from its DIFC branch under the supervision of the Dubai Financial Services Authority.

The second part of the announcement is the more consequential, though it is not yet operational. Standard Chartered has joined a planned integration with LMAX, the London-based currency and crypto marketplace, that would make RLUSD eligible margin on agreed LMAX products. Under a structure the bank calls collateral mirroring, the stablecoin would remain in custody at Standard Chartered while LMAX receives a mirrored record of its value that counts toward a client’s positions. The bank said the arrangement still depends on final documentation, testing and regulatory sign-off, and it gave no date for when clients will be able to post RLUSD as margin.

The design is aimed at the counterparty risk that comes with leaving collateral on a trading venue. If an exchange were to fail under the mirrored model, the client’s tokens would still be held at Standard Chartered, one of 29 banks the Financial Stability Board treats as globally systemically important and subjects to tougher capital requirements. Waqar Chaudry, who leads digital assets within the bank’s securities services business, said institutions want exposure to digital asset markets without weakening the protection around their holdings.

RLUSD, which Ripple launched in December 2024 on Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, is backed by US dollars, US government bonds and cash equivalents. It received approval from the Dubai regulator in June 2025 and has grown to a market value of roughly $2.45 billion, still under 1% of a stablecoin market worth about $306 billion.

The move extends a broader push by the bank into digital assets. Standard Chartered has provided crypto custody in Dubai since 2024, and in July said it had become the first global systemically important bank to let institutions mint and redeem Circle’s USDC directly. The timing and terms of LMAX approval will now determine whether the mirroring model moves from concept to a working margin product.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia eyes 1.2 million bpd pipeline boost within weeks by converting gas line
item.description:
A quick 1.2 million bpd addition to bypass capacity would ease some of the supply-risk premium built into crude, since it widens the route Saudi barrels can take around a disrupted Strait of Hormuz. The bearish oil price read is tempered by execution risk: the same corridor was knocked offline by a drone strike only last month, and Houthi attacks keep the Red Sea leg exposed. Port capacity at Yanbu is the bigger constraint for traders to watch, because extra pipeline volume only reaches the market if loadings can keep pace. Taken together, the plan signals that Riyadh expects disruption at Hormuz to persist, and that is supportive of prices over the longer run even if the near-term supply outlook improves at the margin.

----

Earlier:

  • Big Monday recap ... Oil gains on two fronts as Russia hits Ukraine and Saudi vows Houthi response

---

Riyadh is reaching for the fastest lever it has to get more crude around Hormuz, though the real bottleneck may sit at the Red Sea port rather than in the pipe.

Summary:

  • Saudi Arabia is examining plans to raise pipeline crude export capacity to 10 million bpd, according to comments attributed to Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman
  • He said converting a gas pipeline to carry crude could add 1.2 million bpd within seven to eight weeks
  • The Energy Ministry has said reaching the full 10 million bpd target would take two to three years
  • The 7 million bpd East-West pipeline was shut in September after a drone strike launched from Iraq, and was carrying close to 6 million bpd by 6 October
  • Riyadh has been rerouting around 4 million bpd, roughly 4% of global supply, to Yanbu since the US-Iran war disrupted Hormuz shipments
  • Ship-tracking data suggest Yanbu can load only around 4.5 million bpd, a potential constraint on extra exports

Saudi Arabia is examining plans to raise its pipeline crude export capacity to 10 million barrels per day, with Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman saying the conversion of a gas pipeline to carry crude could add 1.2 million bpd within seven to eight weeks.

The comments point to a fast-track first step toward a longer-term goal. The Saudi Energy Ministry has said it expects lifting oil pipeline capacity to 10 million bpd to take two to three years, so the gas line conversion would deliver a meaningful increase well ahead of any full expansion.

The push reflects how central the East-West pipeline has become to Saudi exports. The line runs from fields and processing facilities near the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and has a capacity of around 7 million bpd. Since the US-Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, Riyadh has been using it to reroute around 4 million bpd to Yanbu, according to Reuters, equivalent to about 4% of global supply.

That route has itself come under attack. The pipeline was shut in September after a drone strike launched from Iraq, which Saudi Arabia blamed on Iraqi militias. Argus reported, citing sources, that three of the line’s 11 pumping stations were damaged, one of them significantly, although the pipeline itself was not. On 6 October, Prince Abdulaziz said flows had recovered to close to 6 million bpd, with operations restarting within about a week of the attack. Separately, Aramco shut its 400,000 bpd Jizan refinery on the Red Sea coast after a Houthi attack in early September.

Expansion talk is not new. Reuters reported earlier, citing sources, that the kingdom was considering adding 1 million to 2 million bpd of East-West capacity, potentially including the ability to carry refined products.

Port capacity may prove the binding constraint. Ship-tracking data indicate Yanbu can load only around 4.5 million bpd, well below the pipeline’s nameplate capacity. Any additional pipeline volumes will therefore depend on matching gains at the terminal end.

The plan also suggests Riyadh is preparing for prolonged disruption at Hormuz, with markets now watching for details on which line would be converted, the timeline for terminal upgrades, and the security of a corridor that has already been struck once.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Standard Chartered custody for Ripple’s RLUSD: what custody and collateral mirroring mean for traders
item.description:
Standard Chartered will now hold Ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, RLUSD, for institutional clients through its branch in the Dubai International Financial Centre. The bank also plans to let those clients use RLUSD as trading collateral at LMAX Group without the tokens ever leaving the bank. That second part is not live yet. Together, though, the two pieces show how traditional finance is trying to fix one of crypto’s oldest problems: what happens to your money when the venue holding it fails.

To see why this matters, it helps to unpack three ideas: stablecoins, custody and collateral.

What happened

The bank announced on Monday that it now supports institutional custody of RLUSD issued on the XRP Ledger. The service runs through its DIFC branch, which is regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority. Separately, Standard Chartered has joined a planned integration with LMAX Group, a London-based marketplace for currencies and crypto, that would make RLUSD eligible collateral on agreed LMAX products.

What is RLUSD?

A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to hold a steady value, in this case $1. RLUSD is backed by US dollars, US government bonds and cash equivalents. Ripple launched it in December 2024 on both Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, a public blockchain closely associated with Ripple. The bank’s new service covers only the XRP Ledger version.

RLUSD has grown to a market value of roughly $2.45 billion. That sounds large, but it is still less than 1% of a stablecoin market worth about $306 billion. It is a small player in a field dominated by much bigger tokens.

What custody actually means

Custody is the unglamorous plumbing of finance. A custodian is a regulated institution that keeps your assets safe and is legally responsible for them. In crypto, that usually means the custodian controls the private keys needed to move the tokens.

There is a trade-off. Handing assets to a custodian adds protection, but it also means the custodian sits between you and your funds. Because it operates under regulation, it can be required to monitor, freeze or restrict assets in its care. For institutions, that oversight is usually a feature rather than a drawback, because their own rules often require assets to be held by a regulated party.

Collateral and the exchange problem

When traders use leverage, they must post collateral, also called margin. This is a safety deposit the trading venue holds against possible losses.

Traditionally in crypto, that collateral sits with the exchange itself. If the exchange collapses, traders can become unsecured creditors waiting to recover their money. The 2022 collapse of FTX made that risk painfully clear to the market.

How collateral mirroring works

Standard Chartered’s answer is what it calls collateral mirroring. Under the planned set-up, the RLUSD stays at the bank. LMAX receives a mirrored record of its value, and that value counts toward the client’s trading positions. The tokens themselves never move to the exchange.

The practical effect is a separation between where you trade and where your assets live. If the exchange ran into trouble, the trader’s collateral would still be sitting at Standard Chartered, one of 29 banks the Financial Stability Board classes as globally systemically important and subjects to stricter capital rules.

The bank’s head of digital assets in securities services, Waqar Chaudry, said institutions want access to digital asset markets without weakening how their assets are protected. That is the core pitch: trade on the venue, keep the money at the bank.

What this does and does not mean

It is worth being precise about what has changed. Custody of RLUSD is live for eligible clients. The LMAX collateral arrangement is only planned. The bank said it still depends on final documentation, testing and regulatory approvals, and it gave no date for when clients could post RLUSD as margin.

This is also not Standard Chartered buying RLUSD or XRP. Offering custody is a service, not an investment. Readers should be careful not to treat it as a direct source of demand for XRP, the separate token linked to the XRP Ledger.

The move does fit a pattern. Standard Chartered has offered crypto custody in Dubai since 2024, and in July it said it became the first global systemically important bank to let institutions mint and redeem Circle’s USDC directly. RLUSD received approval from the Dubai regulator in June 2025.

What to watch next

The key milestone is the LMAX integration going live. Watch for confirmation that testing and regulatory approvals are complete, and which LMAX products will accept RLUSD as collateral.

Also watch whether RLUSD’s market value keeps growing relative to the wider stablecoin market. Bank-grade custody could make it more attractive to institutions, but a move from under 1% to a meaningful share would be the real evidence of demand.

What could change the picture: delays or conditions attached to the LMAX approval, or other large banks offering similar mirroring arrangements for bigger stablecoins, which could leave RLUSD’s advantage short-lived.

The lesson for traders is straightforward. Where your collateral sits matters as much as where you trade. Collateral mirroring is one attempt to separate the two, and it is worth understanding before it becomes standard practice.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan says Q3 earnings will support stocks as growth spreads beyond AI
item.description:
The call argues for broadening rather than narrowing equity exposure, with near-record numbers of stocks seeing accelerating earnings suggesting leadership need not rest on a handful of AI names. For Europe, recent derating in banks and French equities sets a lower bar into results, leaving room for relief rallies if earnings simply hold up. The bond market is the swing factor: a peak in yields as reporting gets under way would remove the main headwind to valuations, while a further leg higher would test the thesis. Companies flagging rising energy costs also tie the earnings outlook back to crude, so any renewed oil spike is a direct risk to European margins.

---

Earlier:

  • US stocks close mixed

--- JPMorgan reckons the headline earnings bar looks scarier than it is, and that once results start rolling in, September’s jitters should give way to fundamentals that still hold up.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan strategists led by Mislav Matejka expect third-quarter earnings to support markets, with strength broadening beyond AI despite investor concern after weeks of volatility
  • S&P 500 consensus sees Q3 EPS growth of 24% on IBES data (30% on FactSet and LSEG after a Meta tax adjustment), falling to 15% excluding Nvidia and Micron and 8% for the median stock
  • European consensus is 19%, dropping to 11% excluding energy, with a median of 9%; median revenue growth is 7% on both sides of the Atlantic
  • Global PMIs hit multi-year highs in the quarter, and JPMorgan’s lead indicator points to at least two more positive reporting seasons
  • European margins are seen around 14% of sales this year, 250 basis points above 2019, with energy likely to beat while miners, China and consumer exposure lag
  • JPMorgan stays positive on European semiconductors, banks, chemicals and industrials, and sees a peak in bond yields opening the way for equity gains into year-end

Third-quarter earnings should reassure investors and act as a support for equities, according to JPMorgan strategists, who say profit strength is broadening beyond artificial intelligence even as many investors fear results will disappoint after weeks of market volatility.

The team, led by Mislav Matejka, said investors already hold a constructive view on earnings, but argued that results will still underpin the market. Expectations look elevated at face value, the strategists said, yet appear more reasonable on closer inspection. Consensus for S&P 500 earnings per share growth in the quarter stands at 24% on IBES data. FactSet and LSEG put the figure at 30% because of an adjustment for a one-off tax charge at Meta. Excluding Nvidia and Micron, the growth hurdle falls to 15%, and for the median stock it drops to 8%.

In Europe, consensus is for 19% growth, easing to 11% once energy is stripped out, with a median of 9%. Median revenue growth is running at 7% for both the S&P 500 and the Stoxx 600.

JPMorgan pointed to global purchasing managers’ indexes, which accelerated during the quarter to multi-year highs and are consistent with strong earnings. The bank’s own lead indicator for earnings is still rising and typically runs about two quarters ahead, which the strategists said suggests at least the next two reporting seasons should be positive. AI continues to carry much of the load in the US, they said, but the share of global stocks with accelerating earnings is close to a record, which should improve the odds of a durable upcycle.

In Europe, margin expansion is doing most of the work, with operating margins projected at around 14% of sales this year, some 250 basis points above 2019 levels. Every sector is improving except staples, autos and software. A weaker euro should help exporters, and energy is likely to surprise to the upside. Miners are a risk, China and consumer exposure may remain soft, and companies are likely to flag rising energy costs.

The strategists also expect strong results from semiconductors and industrials. Banks have derated, meaning their valuation multiples have fallen, by more than 10% in recent weeks but should still report reassuring earnings. French equities have derated by more than 15% even as profits hold up, though the CAC 40 earns three quarters of its revenue outside France.

Looking ahead, JPMorgan said the recent spike in bond yields is nearing oversold territory. If yields peak as the reporting season begins, equities could climb into year-end with risk-on internals, the strategists said. The bank remains positive on European semiconductors, banks, chemicals and industrials, and expects market focus to shift from September’s volatility toward fundamentals that remain supportive. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Hammack says more tightening needed to cool demand, keeps open mind on pace
item.description:
Hammack’s remarks reinforce the hawkish tilt within the Fed and keep the possibility of a back-to-back hike alive, even though markets currently expect a hold in October. Her explicit focus on AI-driven capex and wealth effects puts high-flying tech equities in the crosshairs, since tighter policy aimed at curbing investment and asset-fuelled spending works partly through valuations. The comments should lend support to the dollar and front-end Treasury yields, while also weighing on gold, which has tended to fall as rate hike expectations build. Traders will watch whether other voters echo her view that the inflation fight now targets demand directly rather than the labour market.

---

Hammack wants to take some heat out of a booming economy without burning the labour market, and she is open about which part of demand she would prefer to cool first.

Summary:

  • Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said she believes interest rates need to move higher to restrain demand and bring down inflation, which she sees stuck in a 2.5% to 3.0% range
  • She said she will approach the October 27-28 meeting with an open mind on whether to hike again after September’s increase; markets currently expect a hold
  • Hammack hopes tighter policy can cool corporate investment or wealth-driven consumption without pushing unemployment above the current 4.2%
  • She warned an inflationary psychology may be taking root, with AI-related investment pressures spreading beyond data centres to other firms
  • Business contacts are describing a booming economy rather than preparing to pull back, according to Hammack, who is a voter this year and dissented in July in favour of a hike

Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said on Monday she believes US interest rates need to rise further to restrain demand. She also said she hopes the Fed can bring inflation down without damaging a labour market that remains close to full employment.

In an interview with Reuters, Hammack said demand is being driven both by a rapid pace of corporate investment and by market-driven wealth gains that are supporting consumer spending, factors she sees as keeping inflation lodged in a range of 2.5% to 3.0%. In her view, restrictive monetary policy could cool those forces enough for inflation to fall without unemployment rising beyond the current 4.2%. She said she is not trying to stop growth, only to slow it to a pace that eases pricing pressure. A pullback in either business investment or consumption would help, she added, and restraint on the capital spending side might mean less of the burden falls on consumers.

Hammack said she would go into the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting with an open mind on whether another hike is warranted after September’s increase. She feels more restriction is needed, she said, but considers the timing an open question. Hammack is a voter on rate policy this year and dissented in July in favour of a hike, while investors currently expect the Fed to hold in October. Her remarks are among the most explicit from a Fed official about using restrictive policy to cool demand directly.

With inflation high and the labour market stable, Hammack said the Fed is being challenged on only one side of its mandate. She wants to address inflation deliberately so that employment is not weakened unnecessarily. In her assessment, consumer spending is being held up largely by higher-income households and the wealth effect.

Hammack said business contacts sound more like they are describing a booming economy than preparing to retrench. She is concerned that an inflationary psychology may already be taking root among firms competing for resources, as relentless investment by AI hyperscalers leaves cost a secondary concern. Executives, she said, are planning for inflation to stay high and expect to raise prices faster than their input costs. In her view, the pressure that began with data centres is now spreading more broadly.

Hammack described monetary policy as a single blunt instrument that she intends to use judiciously, in the right amount and at the right speed, while maintaining that more restraint is needed. Her comments leave the October decision finely balanced between market expectations of a pause and a hawkish core of policymakers who see a case for tightening further.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs flags power and compute as two chokepoints in the AI boom
item.description:
The note points investors toward the physical layer of the AI trade, with access to high-voltage power now a tighter constraint than the capital to buy chips. That favours operators that have already secured grid capacity, and it suggests power availability, more than chip supply, could set the pace of new data centre builds through 2027. In software, budgets moving toward data and cybersecurity point to a widening gap between foundational platforms and application vendors, whose pricing models could come under pressure as agents replace human users. The emphasis on core platform returns also implies investors may reward proven monetisation of compute over speculative new revenue lines.

---

In Goldman’s reading of the AI boom, money can buy the GPUs, but power decides who gets to switch them on.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says demand for AI infrastructure keeps outpacing capacity, and the compute supply-demand gap is widening, based on its discussions with tech company management teams
  • A likely slowdown in model training is being offset by rising investment in AI safety and pacing monitoring, which keeps compute demand elevated
  • Leading hyperscalers are securing power contracts for 2028 and beyond because grid capacity for 2026 and 2027 is essentially fully booked
  • Capex is rising on component inflation and the need for more chips, while revenue generated per unit of power has risen by around two-thirds over the past year
  • Goldman sees data and security platforms among the clearest beneficiaries of AI spending, and says application software is increasingly being built for AI agents rather than people
  • Meta is generating two to three times return on investment per megawatt in its core business, and Google is using a full-stack approach spanning custom silicon, cloud, security and distribution

Demand for AI infrastructure continues to run ahead of available capacity, and the bottleneck is moving from chips toward power, according to Goldman Sachs, which drew on recent discussions with the management teams of technology companies.

The bank said the gap between compute supply and demand is widening, driven by new infrastructure requirements and resilient enterprise spending. Goldman expects model training to slow, but it said companies are stepping up investment in AI safety and pacing monitoring, work that needs more computing power and so keeps overall compute demand high.

In Goldman’s view, power has become the defining constraint. Grid capacity for 2026 and 2027 is essentially booked out, the bank said, and leading hyperscalers are therefore moving aggressively to secure power contracts for 2028 and beyond. Goldman argued that having the capital to buy GPUs is no longer enough on its own, and that access to high-voltage energy infrastructure now decides who can expand. Capital expenditure is climbing on component inflation and demand for more chips. Over the same period, revenue generated from each unit of power has risen by around two-thirds compared with earlier price points over the past year.

The bank also described a structural shift in enterprise software. It believes data and security platforms are among the clearest beneficiaries of AI spending, because AI depends on clean, organised and secure data. Chief information officers are increasingly steering budgets toward foundational data layers and cybersecurity tools, aiming to protect data integrity and contain the risks of unsanctioned “shadow AI” use inside organisations.

Application software is going “headless”, meaning it is increasingly being designed for AI agents rather than human users. Goldman said this lets vendors build more powerful AI features into existing platforms and supports industry growth for now. It cautioned, however, that the change could eventually alter how software companies price and monetise their products.

Among the companies it highlighted, Goldman said Meta continues to generate two to three times return on investment per megawatt of power in its core business while exploring new sources of incremental revenue. Google, the bank said, is relying on a full-stack advantage that combines custom silicon, cloud, security and a vast distribution base to drive core monetisation. In that picture, sales of its TPU chips are one part of a broader portfolio strategy.

Goldman concluded that AI monetisation offers substantial optionality. Even so, in its view core platform monetisation remains among the higher-confidence and higher-return uses of compute, which suggests the established platforms that already earn strong returns on their power may stay the more dependable beneficiaries as capacity remains scarce. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

A busier week starts Tuesday

item.title: Big Monday recap ... Oil gains on two fronts as Russia hits Ukraine and Saudi vows Houthi response
item.description:
A two-front geopolitical premium is now embedded in crude, with traders weighing the risk that direct US involvement against the Houthis widens the conflict around Gulf export infrastructure. The multi-year timeline for Saudi pipeline expansion suggests the kingdom’s ability to reroute or offset disrupted flows will stay constrained, reinforcing the tight-supply narrative. In products, extra Russian diesel would ease pressure on middle distillates, but Kyiv’s warning of winter retaliation keeps energy infrastructure risk two-sided. With US-Iran exchanges still stalled, there is little near-term relief for the oil risk premium.

---

On Monday I wrote in despair of the silly narrative doing the rounds supporting gold. And sure enough gold is much lower now. The same narrative was used to 'explain' the fall in oil, and again the narrative was flawed. 

As a trader I am unbothered by flawed narratives, well ... they are welcome really, they help line up liquidity for those with the ability to apply more rational thoughts. But, in my role here at investingLive each day I am bothered by silly narratives, part of my role is to help traders learn to navigate the markets. Hence my post yesterday saying the foundation of gold's up move yesterday rested on weak foundations:

  • Gold edges up in Asia on the energy truce narrative, that looks like a VERY shaky support

I hope it helped some our investingLive traders out. It was hardly rocket science. 

I am positng now as a bit of catch up, a recap of Monday;s oil move. 

---

Crude found support from both ends of the map, as a fragile Russia-Ukraine energy truce cracked and Saudi Arabia lined up retaliation against the Houthis, with Russian diesel talk only briefly taking the edge off.

Summary:

  • WTI and Brent ground higher through Monday’s session on Middle East and Russia-Ukraine tensions, easing slightly from highs into settlement
  • Zelensky said Russia attacked Ukraine after Trump’s US-Russia energy deal announcement, accused Moscow of violating the energy ceasefire and warned Ukraine would respond in winter without an energy truce; power outages were reported after Russian strikes in the east
  • Russia’s Novak said the two governments are discussing supply, flagged scope for additional diesel on global markets and said exports could reach 3 to 3.5 million tons by year-end
  • Saudi Arabia’s energy minister vowed a serious response to deadly Houthi attacks on oil and gas facilities, and Trump said he would decide whether the US joins Saudi strikes on the group
  • Aramco’s CEO warned global crude supply remains severely tight, and the Saudi Energy Ministry expects pipeline capacity expansion to 10 million bpd to take two to three years
  • Iran said messages with the US continue via intermediaries; Washington reportedly accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions via Qatar, which Iran considers insufficient

Oil prices gained on Monday as renewed uncertainty in the Middle East combined with escalating tensions between Russia and Ukraine, with both WTI and Brent grinding higher through the session before easing slightly from their highs into settlement.

On the Russia-Ukraine front, US President Donald Trump announced a US-Russia energy deal on Friday after crude had settled, following up with further combative rhetoric over the weekend. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that Russia had attacked Ukraine after Trump’s announcement, accusing Moscow of breaching the energy ceasefire associated with Trump. He warned that Ukraine would respond during the winter if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire. Power outages were reported overnight in eastern Ukraine following Russian strikes, despite the announcement.

Crude’s late pullback from session highs coincided with comments from Russia’s Novak on a diesel supply arrangement linked to Trump. Novak said the Russian and US governments are in talks on supply and that Russia has scope to make additional diesel available on global markets, adding that Russian diesel exports could reach 3 to 3.5 million tons by year-end.

In the Middle East, Saudi Arabia’s energy minister pledged a serious response to deadly Houthi attacks on the kingdom’s oil and gas facilities, while Trump said he would make a decision on whether the US joins Saudi strikes against the Yemeni group. Supply concerns added to the support, with the chief executive of Saudi Aramco warning that global crude supply remains severely tight. Benchmarks also drew strength from the Saudi Energy Ministry’s view that lifting oil pipeline capacity to 10 million barrels per day will take two to three years. On 6 October, the energy minister said nearly 6 million bpd was flowing through the East-West pipeline, with operations restored around five days after it was hit.

Elsewhere, an Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said exchanges of messages with Washington are continuing through intermediaries, and that Tehran will reply once its review of US positions is complete. The US reportedly accepted some of Iran’s seven conditions in a response passed on via Qatar, though Tehran regards this as insufficient.

Attention now turns to Trump’s decision on joining strikes against the Houthis, the shape of Saudi Arabia’s response, and Iran’s eventual reply, while the risk of winter attacks on energy infrastructure in Ukraine keeps a second source of supply risk in play.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks close mixed
item.description:
The major U.S. stock indices closed mixed to start the week. The Dow industrial average rose 196 points, but the broader indices finished lower, led by a 0.71% decline in the Nasdaq 100.

The modest index moves masked some much larger declines beneath the surface. Ciena and Lumentum fell nearly 10%, while a number of chip, networking and data-center shares lost 4% or more. The S&P 500 was little changed, but holders of those stocks felt considerably more pain.

The session also came with the U.S. cash Treasury market closed for Columbus Day. That left equities without a fresh cash-bond yield signal. Friday’s yields should not be interpreted as a move in rates today.

The concentration of losses in AI infrastructure and related technology shares helps explain the Nasdaq’s underperformance. It also shows why a nearly unchanged S&P does not necessarily mean a quiet trading day.

Earnings and economic data take center stage

The holiday session is the quiet start to a potentially busy week. Third-quarter earnings season gets rolling with major banks and financials, including JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley. Traders will look beyond the earnings headlines for clues on loan demand, credit quality and the health of the consumer.

For technology, ASML and TSMC will provide important updates on semiconductor demand and investment spending. After today’s sharp declines in AI-related shares, their outlooks could help determine whether buyers regain confidence or sellers keep the pressure on.

The economic calendar also brings CPI on Wednesday and PPI on Thursday, along with retail sales this week. Inflation will test the outlook for Fed policy, while retail sales will show whether consumers are still spending despite higher prices. Strong earnings would give buyers something to work with. But hotter inflation could push yields higher and make the job harder—particularly for growth stocks.

Trading takeaway: Look beneath the index

An index is a weighted basket of stocks. Strength in some components can offset sharp losses in others, leaving the headline change looking relatively tame.

For traders, the practical lesson is to check both the broader market and the stock you own. A higher Dow does not establish a bullish bias for a chip stock falling 5% or more. Buyers in that stock still need to reclaim its own resistance levels and stay above them before they can make a stronger case for control.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, October 13, 2026 - RBA minutes due
item.description:
Two releases this week will shape expectations for the Reserve Bank of Australia’s next move: the minutes of its September policy meeting, due Tuesday, and Thursday’s September labour force figures. Both come out at 11:30 am Sydney time, 00:30 GMT (8:30 pm ET the previous evening).

Today we get the minutes. 

In September, the RBA’s Monetary Policy Board raised the cash rate by a quarter point to 4.60%. The decision was unanimous and widely expected, and it was the fourth increase of the cycle. The board said inflation was still too high, reflecting strain on domestic capacity as well as global shocks from the Middle East conflict and the AI investment boom. It acknowledged that the economy was slowing and the jobs market easing. Neither was happening fast enough to return inflation to target within a reasonable timeframe, it said, particularly with oil prices under renewed upward pressure.

CBA says the minutes should show how seriously the board considered keeping rates on hold. It will also be looking for whether they echo the softer tone Governor Michele Bullock struck at her press conference, when she stressed that the four hikes would take time to work through the economy. The bank sees a higher bar for further tightening. Westpac takes a firmer view and forecasts another increase, to 4.85% by December.

The September hike has already weighed on households. Westpac’s consumer sentiment index fell 4.7% to 80.4 in October, close to the weakest readings in the survey’s history.

On jobs, August brought a surprise gain of around 40,000 positions. Unemployment still rose to 4.6%, the highest since late 2021, as participation climbed to 67.1%. Westpac’s forecast matches consensus: 20,000 new jobs in September, with unemployment unchanged. CBA expects a smaller gain of 10,000 and also sees the jobless rate at 4.6%. It warns that changes in the survey sample could make this month’s print noisier than usual, and it expects unemployment to edge higher as growth slows.

The Australian dollar fell on Monday as escalating war in the Middle East, including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, weighed on demand for risk-sensitive currencies. Geopolitics is likely to remain the main driver, but RBA policy is an important underlying factor. The September hike has added some support for the currency through wider interest rate differentials, so a dovish tone in the minutes or a rise in unemployment on Thursday would weaken the case for further tightening and could leave the Australian dollar more exposed. A firmer message from the board would help cushion it.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tension in the releases sent crude oil prices to a new high
item.description:
Buyers regain control, with $93.48 now a key level to hold.

Crude oil pushed to its highest level since late September, with reports of increased Middle East tensions helping fuel the rally. A technical break above a key swing area gave buyers another reason to push higher.

On the hourly chart, the price moved above resistance between $92.29 and $93.48, reaching a high of $94.36 before rotating lower. The current price is near $93.56, with the pullback so far holding above the top of that former resistance area.

That makes $93.48 the immediate risk-defining level for buyers. When resistance is broken, traders want to see it hold as support. Stay above, and the upside remains the path of least resistance. Move back below, and the breakout loses some of its bullish appeal, opening the door for a deeper rotation into the swing area.

The next upside targets come in at:

  • $94.36: Today’s high.

  • $96.50–$97.00: Swing highs from late September.

  • $98.48: Another higher swing high.

Earlier in the session, the picture was much different. Crude fell to $89.61, briefly moving below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages. However, downside momentum quickly faded, and the price snapped back above both averages.

The sellers had their shot. They could not sustain the break. Buyers took back control, with the hourly price action since then showing a largely steady climb.

The broader technical picture also helped set the stage for the rebound. Last week’s low stalled near $86.93, the 50% midpoint of the rally from the early-July low to the September high. Holding that midpoint gave buyers a level to lean against and helped keep the larger rally intact.

U.S. holiday trading may have amplified today’s swings, while Middle East tensions remain a potential source of support. For traders, however, the price levels provide the clearest guide.

The breakout is in place. Now buyers need to defend it. Holding above $93.48 keeps them in control and leaves $94.36 as the next hurdle.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: EURUSD dips to a new low going back to May 2025
item.description:
The EURUSD has extended below last week’s low of 1.11603, reaching 1.1155 today—its lowest level since May 2025. The pair is currently trading near 1.1159.

The sellers got their opening earlier today when the rally stalled at 1.1217, near the falling 100-hour moving average at the time (see blue line on the chart above). The buyers had their shot, but they could not get above that technical ceiling. The subsequent move to a new low keeps the sellers in control.

What comes next on the downside?

The next key target is 1.11296, the 50% midpoint of the rally from the January 2025 low to the January 2026 high. A swing low from mid-May is also near that level, making it an important area to watch.

For beginner traders, that convergence matters: two technical reference points identify the same area where buyers may look to lean against support and define their risk.

A break below—and the ability to stay below—would open the door toward 1.1060, the May 2025 low, with limited support in between.

What would give buyers more hope?

The first step would be a move back above the falling 100-hour moving average, currently near 1.12056 (blue line on the hourly chart at the top of the post). That would ease some of the immediate downside pressure, but buyers would still need to get and stay above the falling 200-hour moving average near 1.12308.

The price has not traded above that longer moving average since September 10, when EURUSD was near 1.1610. That shows how persistent the selling pressure has been.

For now, the technical message remains bearish. Stay below the 100-hour moving average, and sellers retain control. Reclaim it, and buyers have a first step toward a recovery—but the 200-hour moving average remains the next hurdle.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Hammack: Treasury rates are “modest” by historical standards
item.description:
Comments from the Fed’s Hammack cross the wires:

  • Treasury rates right now are “modest” by historic standards.
  • If the economy were to return to a 3% home mortgage it would likely mean something had gone wrong in the economy.
  • The neutral rate is likely higher but it is hard to pin down.
  • Hearing “early warning signs” of a possible problem with inflation expectations.
  • Need to “cool the economy at the margins.”
  • Higher interest rates won’t dissuade hyperscalers, but might influence firms in other industries.
  • The question for the Fed now is how fast to make policy more restrictive.
  • Don’t want to threaten the jobs side of the Fed’s mandate.
  • There is more restraint that is needed; if monetary policy does nothing market conditions would change.
  • Comments from low income workers was first about trading down, now they are beginning to juggle what bills to pay.

Analysis: The message is hawkish. Hammack is framing the debate around how quickly to make policy more restrictive. Her concern about inflation expectations is key. If households and businesses begin to expect persistently higher inflation, bringing inflation back down could become more difficult.

However, she also recognizes the balancing act. Lower-income workers are struggling to pay bills, and she does not want to threaten jobs. For traders, the comments lean toward tighter policy, but leave the pace unresolved. Her view that the neutral rate is likely higher also suggests that today’s rates may provide less restraint than their level alone would imply.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZDUSD sellers press toward key lows. Can they break through?
item.description:
The NZDUSD is one of the biggest movers in trading today, with dollar strength and NZD weakness keeping the sellers in control.

Since the August 21 high at 0.5985, the pair has trended lower, reaching 0.5579 last Monday. That low came within four pips of the November 2025 low at 0.5575.

Since then, the price has waffled up and down, with a corrective high at 0.56256. That puts the recent trading range at less than 50 pips. After a sustained decline, that consolidation tells us the selling has paused. It does not, by itself, signal that the trend has reversed.

Sellers are back near the floor

Today’s decline has taken the price to around 0.5584—just five pips above last Monday’s low.

For traders, the support area at 0.5575–0.5579 is the next key test. Buyers can lean against that area with risk defined below it. Sellers want to see a break below, followed by the ability to stay below, to open the door for further downside momentum.

The next downside targets would include:

  • 0.55388: The 2024 low.

  • 0.5486: The April 8 low.

  • 0.5400: Near the 2020 low.

A break is one thing. Staying below is another. If sellers push through support but the price quickly snaps back above it, the sellers will have had their shot—and missed.

What would give buyers some breathing room?

On a rebound, the first resistance comes near 0.5605, followed by last week’s high area near 0.5626–0.5627.

A move above that ceiling would give buyers a short-term victory and put the falling 100-hour moving average near 0.5644 in play. Getting above—and staying above—that moving average would be another step toward improving the technical picture.

For now, the sellers remain in control. The buyers need to defend the floor and then reclaim resistance. Until they do, a bounce is still a correction within the broader downtrend.

item.title: Gold falls toward hourly moving averages. Can sellers keep control?
item.description:
Gold has rotated lower after reaching a session high of $4,217.19, falling short of the October 2 high at $4,226.83. The price subsequently fell to $4,154.79 and is currently trading near $4,167, down $27.50, or 0.65%.

Reports that Kazakhstan has begun selling gold are attracting attention, while the higher Treasury-yield backdrop is also being cited as a headwind. Ironically, the US treasury market is closed today for the Columbus Day holiday. So although yields are higher, blaming it on higher yields today is kind of a stretch.

Nevertheless, gold pays no interest. When Treasury yields rise, investors can earn more from holding government debt, increasing the opportunity cost of holding gold. That can weigh on demand, although the relationship does not work perfectly every day.

Put the Kazakhstan headline in perspective

The World Gold Council’s September report showed that gold accounted for approximately 75% of Kazakhstan’s reserves. It also showed that the country had accumulated 29 tonnes through July. With that much of its reserves concentrated in gold, some diversification would be understandable. That is a possible explanation, rather than confirmation of the reason for any current sales.

One country selling does not establish a broader central-bank selling trend. The size, timing and purpose of the sales matter.

My take? The headline is another ingredient in the pot that determines price. It may contribute to short-term selling, but I would hesitate to call it a game changer by itself.

The headline gets attention. The technicals define the next test.

Today’s high fell short of the October high. Buyers had their shot at extending toward that level, but could not get there before the price rotated lower. That gives sellers an initial victory.

The decline has now brought two important technical levels into play:

  • 200-hour moving average: $4,167.60

  • 100-hour moving average: $4,152.92

At a price near $4,167, gold is just below the 200-hour moving average but remains above the 100-hour moving average. Today’s low at $4,154.79 also held just above that lower moving average.

That distinction matters. Sellers have made progress, but they have more work to do.

Moving averages give traders reference points for judging control and defining risk. They do not guarantee that support will hold. The useful information comes from how the price behaves around them.

What would strengthen the bearish case?

For sellers, staying below the 200-hour moving average would keep the immediate pressure on. The next step would be a break below the 100-hour moving average at $4,152.92.

Getting below both—and staying below—would tilt the technical bias more to the downside.

A brief dip below support followed by a quick recovery would be less convincing. Traders should watch for follow-through: can the price remain below the broken level, and do rebounds find sellers against it?

What would give buyers another opportunity?

For buyers, the first job is to defend the 100-hour moving average. The next is to reclaim the 200-hour moving average at $4,167.60 and stay above it.

That would suggest the selling pressure is easing and give buyers a chance to rotate back toward today’s high at $4,217.19, followed by the October high at $4,226.83.

Holding support is a start. Reclaiming the higher moving average would strengthen the buyers’ case.

Holidays deserve a different lens

Today is a U.S. bond-market holiday in observance of Columbus Day.

Holiday participation can be thinner, allowing a headline to produce a larger price reaction than it might during a busier session. That is a possibility, not proof that today’s move is exaggerated.

For traders, the lesson is to respect the headline while watching whether the market can sustain the move through a meaningful technical level.

The news can provide the shove and that shove may be exaggerated today. The technicals help us judge whether buyers or sellers are taking control—and give us a level against which to define and limit risk.

For gold, the next battle is clear: $4,152.92 below and $4,167.60 above. Watch which side the price breaks, whether it stays there, and whether momentum follows.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin buyers had their shot above the 200-hour MA. They missed.
item.description:
Bitcoin is trading near its session low at $82,389 after reaching a high of $84,254 earlier today.

That high took the price above the 200-hour moving average (green line), currently at $83,877. The break gave buyers an opportunity to build upside momentum. Instead, the move failed, buyers turned to sellers, and the price rotated lower.

The decline has since taken bitcoin below its 100-hour moving average at $82,786, giving sellers another short-term technical victory.

Can they keep the pressure on?

24 days of range trading

Looking at the bigger picture, bitcoin has spent the last 24 days—since September 18—trading between $80,106 and $87,374. There has been plenty of up-and-down price action, but no sustained break from that range.

Last Tuesday, buyers made another run toward the upper extreme but stalled ahead of the target. The subsequent reversal took the price below both the 100- and 200-hour moving averages.

Apart from brief breaks above the 200-hour moving average on Sunday and again today, the price has remained below that indicator, keeping the technical bias more bearish.

What sellers need to do next

On the downside, the price is now within a swing area between $81,183 and $82,653. Sellers need to push below the lower boundary at $81,183 to open the door for a test of $80,106—the September 20 low that was revisited last week.

Break below $80,106 and stay below, and sellers would finally have a move outside the broader trading range, opening the door for further downside momentum.

Until then, support still needs to be broken. Sellers have more work to do.

What buyers need to reclaim

For buyers, the first step is to reclaim the 100-hour moving average at $82,786. Above that, the 200-hour moving average at $83,877 remains the key hurdle. Getting above and staying above that level would give buyers another opportunity to take back control.

The buyers had their shot today. They missed. Sellers have the advantage below the hourly moving averages, but they still need to break support to turn that advantage into a bigger move lower.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: EUR/USD consolidates at the lows as France's budget and US CPI remain in focus
item.description:
The US dollar has been supported recently despite a dovish repricing triggered by Fed’s Williams and Fed’s Jefferson comments that pushed back against expectations of a rate hike in October.

The main reason were risk-off flows into the greenback due to European debt concerns. The focus has been particularly on France, where political uncertainty and concerns over the country's large fiscal deficit have recently pushed French government bond yields higher and widened the spread over German Bunds to its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis.

A stabilization in French spreads could allow some of the euro's risk premium to unwind and trigger a pullback in the US dollar, while further widening and contagion to other countries would likely keep the greenback supported.

Moreover, the US-Iran negotiations continue to be at a stalemate but at least Trump ruled out new strikes before the November elections last week. This week, we also have the US CPI report on the agenda, which could trigger big moves in the markets.

A hotter than expected core CPI could bring a rate hike in October back on the table and give the US dollar a boost. A soft report, on the other hand, will likely weigh on the greenback in the short-term on a fall in Treasury yields.

On the EUR side, the probabilities of an ECB rate hike in October have faded following the sharp widening in the French-German bond spread, as policymakers are likely to remain cautious about adding further pressure to already fragile financial markets.

However, markets still expect the ECB to raise rates in December, reflecting persistent inflationary pressures due to higher energy prices. In terms of economic data, the latest Eurozone CPI showed headline inflation surging to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, largely due to higher energy prices. Core inflation remained relatively contained, edging up to 2.5% from 2.4%.

Looking ahead, energy prices and developments in the Middle East will remain important drivers of the inflation outlook. Any sustained decline in energy prices could reduce near-term inflation pressure and give the ECB more room to delay further tightening. This would also be positive for the euro on improved risk sentiment and lower Fed rate hike expectations.

The euro will also remain sensitive to developments in the bond market, particularly the French-German spread. France’s government has proposed a 2027 budget targeting a deficit of 5.0% of GDP, supported by spending restraint and higher tax revenues. This is lower than the previously 5.4% and helped ease market concerns somewhat. However, the plan still faces parliamentary hurdles, and Eurozone finance ministers and the ECB have urged France to pass a credible budget to restore market confidence.

Traders will keep a close eye on France where improvements would be positive for the euro, while negative outcomes will likely continue to weigh on the single currency.

 

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that EURUSDhas been selling off heavily in the past weeks on France’s debt woes. The nearest key support is around the 1.1067 level. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the level, to position for a recovery into the major downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into the 1.08 handle next.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the selloff since early September. The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break to start positioning into the major downward trendline, with the 1.1285 level as the first target.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we can see that the pair has been bottoming out since the French proposed budget deficit for 2027 got lowered to 5.0% from 5.4%. We have a support zone around the 1.1160 level. The buyers will likely continue to step in around the support, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting a break above the trendline and new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

On Wednesday we have the US CPI report. On Thursday, we get the US PPI, the US Retail Sales and the latest US Jobless Claims figures. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

It was a quieter session in European morning trade today as broader markets have to contend with a US partial market holiday to start the new week.

The US bond market is closed in observance of Columbus day and while the stock market remains open, traders and investors are still missing one key piece of the puzzle in broader markets today. That is especially the case since surging Treasury yields have been a major driver of trading sentiment over the past few weeks.

As such, the absence of a key signal for broader markets is providing some room for a bit of a breather. But at the same time, thinner liquidity conditions could also lead to some exacerbated price moves as we get things going in the new week.

Oil prices were down early on but recovered well to be up over 1% on the day currently. Hopes of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire helped to drag prices down in the early stages before the focus turned back towards tensions in the Middle East, where supply disruptions continue to weigh on the market mood. WTI crude was down to just under $90 earlier in the day but is trading back up to near $93 currently.

Meanwhile, the dollar is holding slightly firmer as it posts a light advance against the rest of the major currencies bloc. USD/JPY is up 0.2% to 158.60 while EUR/USD is down 0.2% to 1.1175, so the gains are not anything to shout about for the time being.

As for equities, European stocks are enjoying a modest start after a rough period in trading last week. While regional bond yields are still keeping the pressure on, investors are able to take some comfort from the broader market mood - at least for now. Looking to US futures, it's a bit more of a mixed mood with tech shares sagging a little ahead of the open later. S&P 500 futures are up 0.1% while Nasdaq futures are down 0.2% so far on the day.

And in the commodities space, gold is also down 0.5% to $4,170 after another technical rejection from the $4,200-20 region once again.
